name: Wayâna
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.

catalog_locator: §2.4.1 'Intonational units and the lack of stress', p. 91 main statement + fn. 65; pp. 97-98 conclusion; p. 9 fn. 1 (p. 27); p. 106 (p. 124) sound-symbolic caveat; §2.4 opens p. 90.
catalog_quote: [p. 91] This simple organization is the most basic suprasegmental pattern found in Wayâna, applying even at the word level. This means that Wayâna prosody there exist no properties that systematically isolate more prominent syllables in a word. As a consequence, we state that stress does not exist in the Wayâna words. ... Wayâna seems to be a language of a rarer type. None of the known four phonetic correlates of stress clearly isolate a unique syllable within a word. There are no cases of vowels being systematically reduced in any environment (though onomatopoeic words, still under investigation, may prove to present exceptional cases). As for the other three phonetic correlates, length, pitch, and amplitude, there is a more or less a random distribution of them, as they may not necessarily occur all together on a same syllable. [pp. 97-98] While English and Tiriyó present prominent stressed syllables, Wayâna does not seem to do so, as the variation between syllables is very small, and no particular syllable in a word is consistently prominent. [p. 9 fn. 1] Stress is not indicated in the examples since it is not distinctive in the language.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (454-page UMI scan, no text; the PDF's metadata/extracted text confirm image-only) and rendered pp. 27, 109, 115-116 myself with page render rather than trusting the scanned files. Offset 18 is right: PDF 109 carries printed page number 91, PDF 27 = p. 9, PDF 116 = p. 98. On p. 91 the passage reads exactly: "This simple organization is the most basic suprasegmental pattern found in Wayâna, applying even at the word level. This means that Wayâna prosody there exist no properties that systematically isolate more prominent syllables in a word. As a consequence, we state that stress does not exist in the Wayâna words.[fn 65]" — identical to the reported quote except the circumflex in Way…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Wayana has no word stress: none of the phonetic correlates (length, pitch, amplitude, vowel reduction) consistently single out one syllable of a word; length, pitch and intensity peaks fall on different syllables from token to token, there is no vowel reduction, and utterances (words in isolation and phrases alike) are shaped only by a utterance-final pitch rise (non-final/question) or fall (final). Tavares contrasts this explicitly with Tiriyó's iambic rhythmic stress (Meira 1999). Final syllables that end in a rising pitch tend to be the longest, but this is intonational, not stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None; the source denies any word-level prominence at all, so no secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Sound-symbolic (onomatopoeic) words: fn. 5 p. 91 and p. 106 say some examples 'suggest that there may be a fixed position for a most prominent syllable' in that class, but the investigation was not carried out. The author also flags that a fuller study of intonational units is still needed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level and phrase level treated together: instrumental measurements (vowel length in ms, F0 range, amplitude) of words in isolation (e.g. akisita, umpoj, imta, jempatak, emehna, tijomtaj) and of a two-word phrase eputpï patuku show the same organisation; the phonological word is equated with the grammatical word (2.4.2). Intonation: rising/steady pitch = utterance non-final or question; falling pitch = utterance final.
new_statements.identity_note: Tavares 2006 (Glottolog title variant 'A grammar of Wayana (Brazil)') describes the Wayana of Brazil (Pará; Wayana-Aparai community); Jackson 1972 and Grimes 1972 describe Suriname Wayana (Tapanahoni and Lawa rivers). Glottolog waya1269 has no dialect subdivisions; all sources fall under it. The no-stress statement is first-hand for the Brazilian variety; Camargo 1996 (French Guiana side) not checked.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The grammar argues there is no word stress at all, not even at a surface level: no syllable in a word is consistently singled out by length, pitch, intensity or vowel quality; the only systematic suprasegmental pattern is utterance-level intonation (rising or steady pitch when more is to come, falling pitch at the end of an utterance), which applies to words and phrases alike; the grammatical word and the phonological word are treated as identical because no prosodic domain beyond the grammatical word is detectable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not applicable; the author denies any word-level prominence, so no secondary stress is described.
new_statements.exceptions: Sound-symbolic (onomatopoeic) words are flagged as a possible exception: p. 91 fn. 65 'An investigation on sound symbolic words may reveal stress to operate in that domain (cf. 2.6)'; and p. 106: 'Finally, the present study is lacking a discussion on stress patterns in sound symbolic words. Examples such as (241 b and d) above suggest that there may be a fixed position for a most prominent syllable. This investigation, however, was not carried out in the work.' Also p. 91: vowel reduction is absent 'though onomatopoeic words, still under investigation, may prove to present exceptional cases'. Final syllables ending in a rising pitch tend to be the longest (p. 93), but this is intonational, not stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Tavares describes the Wayâna of the Paru (Parú de Leste) River, Brazil (she notes Paru River speakers' pronunciations at p. 10 fn. 2); the same language is spoken in Suriname and French Guiana, and Camargo's unread 1996 article is based on French Guiana / Maroni data. The catalog head 'Wayâna' with no rule is the same language.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record has an empty rule; the existing statement (Tavares 2006, sec. 2.4.1) concludes that word stress does not exist in Wayana (no properties systematically isolate a prominent syllable; prominence is intonational/phrase-level). Camargo 1996 asserts the opposite type: a word-level main accent plus secondary accents. The contradiction is in type (stress present vs absent), not placement, since Camargo gives no placement and labels her claim provisional ('analyse.. en cours'). Her own variable accent marks (final ~ penultimate ~ initial on comparable word shapes) are, if anything, consistent with Tavares's later finding that no fixed word-level prominence exists. Same variety as…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Camargo asserts that the Wayana word carries one main accent plus one or more secondary accents (number depending on word length), but explicitly defers the analysis of accent and never states where the main accent falls. Accent is used throughout as a conditioning environment (vowel laxing /i ï u/ > [I Ï µ] and /ε ç/ > [´ P], /a/ > [å] in unaccented syllables; /w/ > [ß] in unaccented syllables; regressive nasalization of /a/ before a nasal onset in accented syllables). Her phonetic transcriptions mark the accent (') variably: final in e.g. /muRε/ [mµ'Rε], /aRuwa/ [åRµ'wa], /wεwε/ [wε'wε], /akçn/ [a'kP)n], /wapçt/ [ßa'pçt]; penultimate in /taRani/ [ta'Rå)ni], /wajana/ [ßå'jå)nå], /sipaRi/ [_i'paRI], /pakçRç/ [pa'kçRç]; initial in /juju/ ['jujµ], /waRa maRi/ ['waRå 'maRI]; two marks in /ipçk´nma/ [i'pçk´)'må)]. No placement rule is given.
new_statements.secondary_stress: States that there are one or more secondary accents per word depending on word length (fn. 5); no positions given. One transcription shows two accent marks: /ipçk´nma/ > [i'pçk´)'må)] 'tres bien'.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; notes that neutralizations/laxing occur 'surtout en debit rapide et en syllabe non-accentuee', and that morpheme-level vowel harmony (sec. 1.2.3) overrides the accent-conditioned laxing rule so that accented and unaccented vowels share the same ATR value.
new_statements.identity_note: Camargo's data were collected on the Paru de Leste, Brazil (three field trips 1993-1996; village Suwi Suwi min mentioned for one nasalization variant); she cites De Goeje's Surinam Wayana only for comparison. Tavares 2006 likewise worked along the Paru River in Brazil, so both sources describe Brazilian Wayana, not the Maroni/Lawa (French Guiana/Surinam) varieties.

readall_conflicts: Camargo 1996 (fn. 5, p. 5) states provisionally that the Wayana word has a main accent and one or more secondary accents depending on word length, with the accent analysis 'in progress' and no placement given; she uses accented vs unaccented syllable as the conditioning environment for vowel laxing, /w/-spirantization and /a/-nasalization. Tavares 2006 (sec. 2.4.1 'Intonational units and the lack of stress', pp. 90-98; fn. 1 p. 9), the existing statement of record, concludes from pitch/intensity/duration measurements that no syllable is systematically more prominent within the word and that stress does not exist in Wayana words, prominence being a property of intonational units. The two therefore disagree on whether word stress exists at all. Camargo's claim is a footnote in a preliminary segmental study and her own transcriptions place the accent mark inconsistently (final /muRε/ [mµ'Rε], /aRuwa/ [åRµ'wa]; penultimate /taRani/ [ta'Rå)ni], /wajana/ [ßå'jå)nå]; initial /juju/ ['jujµ]), so the detailed later analysis (Tavares) remains the better-supported reading; both describe the same variety (Paru de Leste, Brazil).
